<reason>A very close debate. CON's strongest line was burden-shifting: the motion contains a comparative "more than most successful people admit," and CON extracted PRO's honest concession that it has no representative survey. But CON's own evidence on the admission clause (speeches, bestsellers, "check your privilege") was conceded to be non-representative, so that clause ends roughly symmetric, and PRO correctly flagged this. On the first clause, PRO's core move—that accurate selection on competence can still transmit class because resources produce the competence—was never squarely refuted; CON's opening framing (if the admitted are strongest, meritocracy is "simply true") was directly dismantled in A2.1. PRO also handled CON's one number well: half an advantage persisting per generation is not "evaporating," and a population average cannot rule out elite-gateway persistence; CON's reply that elites would "drag the average" is weak reasoning. PRO answered both pressure questions directly, offered a concrete threshold concept and a concrete admission statement, defusing the unfalsifiability charge honestly. CON was rhetorically sharper and framed the closing cleanly, but two clipped turns and some contestable assertions (elites regress sharply at the top) cost it. PRO edges it on argument survival and epistemic discipline.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A2.1/A4.4 versus B2.3–B2.4: CON's "a machine that loses half its input is a weak machine" was the debate's most memorable framing, but PRO's counter that half an advantage surviving is substantial persistence, that children can fall below wealthy parents while staying far above disadvantaged peers, and that population mobility doesn't measure elite gateways, largely neutralized CON's only quantitative evidence.</best_rebuttal>
